title: The Cliff and the Airplane: Berkeley, Confinity, LinkedIn, and the Files
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Stanford Hospital, Palo Alto: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested; both the Academy of Achievement profile and Wikipedia give 5 August 1967, Palo Alto. The pin is Stanford University Medical Center at 500 Pasteur Drive, not the downtown Palo Alto coordinate carried in some working notes, which sits three kilometres away.
stops.campa: Reid Garrett Hoffman is born at the Stanford University Medical Center on Pasteur Drive, the son of two lawyers, Deanna Ruth Rutter and William Parker Hoffman Jr. His father is a Stanford law student at the time, which is why the birth happens on this campus and not another hospital. The birth record carries a Peninsula address, the first of a long series of them, and the only one chosen for him rather than by him. The parents separate while he is still an infant. The household he is carried home to does not last a year.
suggested_refs: Stanford University Medical Center, 500 Pasteur Drive, Palo Alto
sources: Academy of Achievement, achiever profile, achievement.org/achiever/reid-hoffman/

stops.name: Sunnyvale: the grandparents' house
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the episode rests on Nicholas Lemann's New Yorker profile 'The Network Man' (12 October 2015) as relayed by the background dossier, which was not re-fetched in this pass. The date orders the segment and is not attested.
stops.campa: After the separation his mother carries him north to Alaska for a season and then back down to her own parents' house in Sunnyvale, twenty minutes from the hospital he was born in. He is not yet two. The household that takes them in is a grandparents' household, ordinary, in a valley of orchards that has not yet been renamed for silicon. This stretch of his childhood survives only in a magazine profile written forty-eight years later, from his own account.
suggested_refs: Nicholas Lemann, 'The Network Man,' The New Yorker, 12 October 2015

stops.name: Mill Valley: the father's second household
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; dossier-only, after Lemann. No year is given by any source reached here, and the date is set to order the segment.
stops.campa: His father remarries and the boy crosses the bay to Mill Valley, under Mount Tamalpais, into a second household with a second set of rules. He shuttles between parents. The custody arrangements of the early 1970s put a child on bridges, and the record of these years is thin: no school names, no addresses, no anecdotes anyone has written down, only the fact of two houses and the road between them. What is known is where it ends. The family settles in Berkeley, and Berkeley is where he is raised.
suggested_refs: Lemann, 'The Network Man,' on the divided households of the early 1970s

stops.name: Berkeley: the public schools
stops.date_confidence: attested as a fact, inferred as to date; achievement.org states he was raised in Berkeley and attended its public schools through junior high at the Martin Luther King school. No year for any particular grade is given, and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Berkeley in the 1970s raises him: the public schools, junior high at the Martin Luther King school, a city where politics are argued on the sidewalk and a bright child can find adults willing to take his argument seriously. The house is not a wealthy one. No source reached here keeps a teacher's name or a grade from any of these years. What survives is the habit the city rewards, and which he will be using on his own parents before he is fifteen: if you want a thing, build the case for it.
suggested_refs: Martin Luther King Jr. Middle School, Berkeley Unified School District
sources: Academy of Achievement, achiever profile, achievement.org

stops.name: Oakland: the critique carried to Chaosium
stops.date_confidence: core attested, detail unverified; Wikipedia states plainly that he was an editor at the game company Chaosium, then based in Oakland. The 1982 Borderlands credit and the fee of 127 dollars come from a company archival account relayed by the dossier and were not re-fetched here. The dossier itself notes he was fourteen through most of 1982.
stops.campa: Before he leaves California, a preteen walks into the offices of Chaosium, publisher of the role-playing game RuneQuest, carrying a marked-up critique of rules he has been playing. The designer Steve Perrin reads it. Instead of humoring the boy, the company gives him paid editorial work, and he becomes, at an age when most contributors are readers, an editor at a game company. A house archive is said to credit him in the 1982 Borderlands box for a fee of one hundred and twenty-seven dollars.
suggested_refs: Chaosium's RuneQuest line and the 1982 Borderlands boxed set
sources: reid_hoffman.dossier.md, citing a Chaosium archival account

stops.name: The College Preparatory School, Oakland: the campaign to leave
stops.date_confidence: attested as a fact, inferred as to date; achievement.org places him at the College Preparatory School before boarding school. No enrolment year is given by any source reached here, and the year set here overlaps the Putney span in the dossier without resolving it.
stops.campa: He is sent to the College Preparatory School on the Berkeley and Oakland line, a small independent school with a reputation for taking adolescents at their word. He does not stay. Having read about a place in Vermont where students milk cows and forge iron between Latin classes, he mounts a campaign on his own family to be sent three thousand miles east to it, and wins the argument. The campaign is the earliest documented instance of the thing he will later sell as a skill. He is not yet fifteen when he leaves California.
suggested_refs: The College Preparatory School, Broadway, Oakland
sources: Academy of Achievement, achiever profile, achievement.org

stops.name: The Putney School, Vermont: the forge and the sugarhouse
stops.date_confidence: attendance attested by Wikipedia and achievement.org; the 1981-1985 span comes from the dossier and could not be confirmed in either source, though the 1985 graduation is firm. The pin is the Putney School's own geotag at 418 Houghton Brook Road, not the open country four kilometres south carried in working notes.
stops.campa: The Putney School sits on a hill above the West River in southern Vermont and runs on the labor of its students: morning milking, the sugarhouse in March, the forge, the wood shop, academics in between. A Californian arrives who has argued his way here, three thousand miles from either of his parents' houses. He learns to shoe a horse and to boil sap, and he lives among people who do not care what his father does. He will describe companies in the vocabulary of the forge and the barn for the rest of his working life. He graduates in 1985.
stops.quote: I think of myself as a mystical atheist, which is neither the full atheist category nor any religious category.
stops.quote_source: Reid Hoffman, in conversation with Tyler Cowen, Conversations with Tyler, January 2020
suggested_refs: The Putney School farm, forge, and sugarhouse, Putney, Vermont
sources: Academy of Achievement, achiever profile, achievement.org

stops.name: Stanford University: Symbolic Systems and a student senate quarrel
stops.date_confidence: attested; the 1990 B.S. with distinction is given by both Wikipedia and achievement.org, and the 1985 matriculation follows from it. That he met Peter Thiel through student politics and Michelle Yee as an undergraduate is attested in the same two sources.
stops.campa: He enters Stanford and finds Symbolic Systems, a program that puts philosophy, linguistics, computer science, and psychology in one room and asks what a mind is. It is the exact shape of his appetite. He argues politics in the student senate with a conservative classmate named Peter Thiel, who is waging a campaign of his own against the university's speech rules; the argument does not end and neither does the acquaintance. He meets Michelle Yee here. He takes the degree with distinction in 1990, intending to become a public intellectual.
stops.quote: Maybe I mask it better. That's my Straussian element, that I hide my weirdness.
stops.quote_source: Reid Hoffman, in conversation with Tyler Cowen, Conversations with Tyler, January 2020
suggested_refs: Stanford's Symbolic Systems Program, founded 1986

stops.name: Wolfson College, Oxford: the Marshall Scholarship
stops.date_confidence: attested; both sources give a Marshall Scholarship to Oxford with a 1993 completion. The pin is Wolfson College's own geotag on Linton Road, correcting a working coordinate that drifted four hundred metres east into Norham Manor.
stops.campa: A Marshall Scholarship carries him to Oxford and to Wolfson College on Linton Road, a graduate college of flat modern brick beside the Cherwell, founded for people who arrive already formed. He reads philosophy. The plan is explicit and he has stated it in application after application: he will write, he will teach, he will be the kind of thinker who changes how a country thinks. Two years of the actual work of academic philosophy are enough to show him what the profession is. Then he starts counting the readers.
suggested_refs: The Marshall Scholarship scheme, founded 1953 in acknowledgement of the Marshall Plan
sources: Academy of Achievement, achiever profile, achievement.org

stops.name: Oxford: the degree taken and the profession refused
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day set to order the segment. The credential's name is contradicted between sources and left so: corporate filings call it an M.A., later biographical accounts an M.St. The Academy of Achievement profile itself carries the discrepancy.
stops.campa: He takes the degree in 1993 and leaves the university without applying for a doctorate. The reason he gives afterward is not disillusionment but arithmetic: a monograph reaches a few hundred readers, and he wants an instrument that reaches millions. The philosophy does not leave him. What leaves is the plan to make a living at it. He goes home to California to look for the instrument, twenty-six years old, with no company, no product, no capital, and a graduate degree in a discipline he has just declined to practise.
stops.quote: And then I fairly quickly realized that philosophical scholarship wasn't interesting to me because it didn't have a broad enough impact.
stops.quote_source: Reid Hoffman, interview transcript, Academy of Achievement
suggested_refs: Wolfson College, Oxford, graduate register for 1993
sources: Academy of Achievement, achiever profile and interview transcript, achievement.org

stops.name: Apple Computer, Cupertino: eWorld and its shutdown
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged, not resolved: Wikipedia gives the Apple employment as 1994-1996, while achievement.org places it at 1995-1996 and says he left in February 1996. The February 1996 departure is common to both. eWorld's own shutdown on 31 March 1996 is separately attested.
stops.campa: He joins Apple's user-experience group and is put on eWorld, the company's own online service: a cartoon town on a dial-up connection, with buildings you clicked to reach mail, news, and a message board. It has a few tens of thousands of subscribers against America Online's millions. He learns there what a network product is and what it costs to lose one. He leaves Apple in February 1996. eWorld is switched off on the thirty-first of March, weeks after his desk is cleared.
suggested_refs: Apple's eWorld service, 1994-1996, and its migration of users toward America Online
sources: Academy of Achievement, achiever profile, achievement.org

stops.name: Fujitsu, the San Jose area: learning to ship
stops.date_confidence: attested to a range, not a month; achievement.org gives 1996-1997, and the dossier narrows it to February 1996 through July 1997 from PayPal filing text. The month here orders the segment. The office location is not established by any source reached in this pass.
stops.campa: He goes to Fujitsu next and takes a product-management job he does not want for its own sake. The reasoning is stated plainly in every account he gives: he has decided to found a company, he has never shipped a product to a schedule, and he will not learn that on his own money. It is an apprenticeship taken deliberately, on someone else's payroll, with an end date already in mind. He stays roughly seventeen months. Which office he sat in is not established by any source reached here.
suggested_refs: Fujitsu America's Silicon Valley operations in the mid-1990s
sources: Academy of Achievement, achiever profile, achievement.org

stops.name: Silicon Valley: SocialNet, the failure he keeps
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; achievement.org gives SocialNet founded July 1997 and financed November 1997, correcting a working note that had put the founding in August. The precise company address is not established in any source reached here.
stops.campa: In July 1997 he founds Relationships.com, renamed SocialNet, a service for matching people to each other: dates, tennis partners, roommates. Financing arrives in November. The idea is early by roughly a decade and the execution is worse than the idea, and he will spend twenty years telling audiences about it as his instructive failure, the one he was allowed to survive. The conclusion he carries out of the wreck is about identity rather than about matching, and he will not act on it for another five years.
stops.quote: One of the metaphors I use for entrepreneurship is you jump off a cliff and you assemble an airplane on the way down.
stops.quote_source: Reid Hoffman, interview transcript, Academy of Achievement
suggested_refs: SocialNet.com, incorporated as Relationships.com, 1997
sources: Academy of Achievement, achiever profile, achievement.org

stops.name: Palo Alto: a seat on Confinity's board
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; Wikipedia records him as a board member at Confinity's founding, and the December 1998 date is common to the dossier and the atlas files for the same events. The coordinate is the canonical Palo Alto pin shared byte for byte with peter_thiel.journey.json, max_levchin.journey.json and elon_musk.journey.json.
stops.campa: Peter Thiel, running a small Palo Alto company called Confinity with Max Levchin, asks his old Stanford adversary onto the board in December 1998. The company is building cryptographic money transfer for handheld computers, a product almost nobody wants, which will mutate into a way to pay strangers on an auction site, which almost everybody wants. Hoffman keeps SocialNet going and sits on the board on the side. He is a director of the company for a year before he works there.

stops.name: Palo Alto: full time at PayPal
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; both Wikipedia and achievement.org give a January 2000 full-time start. The title is contradicted between accounts and is left unresolved in the campa rather than adjudicated here.
stops.campa: In January 2000 he closes his own company and joins full time. The accounts disagree about what he was: Wikipedia and the Academy of Achievement both make him chief operating officer that January, with a senior vice presidency for business development following in June, while some later profiles reverse the order. PayPal's own securities filings would settle it and were not read for this file. His actual work is neither title. While the engineers build, he negotiates with the banks, with the card networks, and with the regulators of fifty separate states, one state at a time.

stops.name: North First Street, San Jose: the sale to eBay
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia's PayPal article gives the eBay acquisition as closing 3 October 2002 for 1.5 billion dollars in stock, announced 8 July. A working note giving June 2002 was wrong by four months. The headquarters coordinate is inherited from elon_musk.journey.json.
stops.campa: PayPal moves to North First Street in San Jose, goes public in February 2002, and on the third of October is bought by eBay for a billion and a half dollars in stock. The people in that building scatter with money and a shared alumni claim: Peter Thiel, Max Levchin, Elon Musk, and Hoffman among them. A Fortune photographer will pose them five years later in mafia dress, without Musk, who is in Chicago collecting an award. Hoffman dislikes the word mafia and proposes network instead.
stops.quote: I actually think that the notion of capitalism is one of the world's leading interesting technologies, but it's not a particularly good philosophy.
stops.quote_source: Reid Hoffman, in conversation with Tyler Cowen, Conversations with Tyler, January 2020
suggested_refs: Jeffrey M. O'Brien, 'The PayPal Mafia,' Fortune, November 2007, and its group portrait

segments.name: LinkedIn, and the Sale to Redmond

stops.name: Mountain View: LinkedIn incorporated in a living room
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia's LinkedIn article gives a founding date of 10 December 2002, and achievement.org describes the organizing work beginning in his living room in the last month of 2002. A working note offering November 2002 as a rival date is not supported by either source.
stops.campa: He starts the next company before the eBay money clears, in his own living room in December 2002, with Allen Blue, Konstantin Guericke, Eric Ly, and Jean-Luc Vaillant. The premise is the conclusion he drew from SocialNet: not that people want to be matched, but that people want a professional self that exists in public and belongs to them rather than to an employer. The company is incorporated on the tenth of December, five founders and a room with the furniture pushed back. He is thirty-five.
stops.quote: That everyone should have a public professional identity. It would help transform their work life...
stops.quote_source: Reid Hoffman, interview transcript, Academy of Achievement
suggested_refs: LinkedIn Corporation's California incorporation record, 10 December 2002
sources: Academy of Achievement, achiever profile, achievement.org

stops.name: Mountain View: the site opens
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia's LinkedIn article gives the public launch as 5 May 2003.
stops.campa: The site opens to the public on the fifth of May 2003. A professional network is worth nothing until the people you actually work with are already on it, and the only route through that problem is to survive the years when they are not. Within a decade the thing will hold the working record of most of the white-collar world. None of that is visible in May 2003, when what the founders have is an address book that has to reach a certain size before it does anything at all. Invitations go out one at a time.
suggested_refs: The LinkedIn launch announcement, 5 May 2003

stops.name: Sand Hill Road, Menlo Park: Greylock and the Discovery Fund
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; Wikipedia and achievement.org both give a 2009 arrival at Greylock Partners with a 20 million dollar discovery fund. Month and day order the segment. The Sand Hill Road office address is general knowledge and was not independently re-verified.
stops.campa: He joins Greylock Partners on Sand Hill Road and brings a twenty million dollar discovery fund with him, money for bets too early to be argued through a partners' meeting. He is now on both sides of the table at once, founder and financier, and the network he built as a product becomes the instrument of the job: he can reach anyone. The Airbnb Series A comes out of this desk, against the general opinion that nobody would sleep in a stranger's apartment.
stops.quote: The company, deploying scalable technology, is the primary modern instrument of human progress.
stops.quote_source: Reid Hoffman, 'Faith in the Possible,' reidhoffman.substack.com
suggested_refs: Greylock Partners, 2550 Sand Hill Road, Menlo Park
sources: Academy of Achievement, achiever profile, achievement.org

stops.name: New York Stock Exchange: LNKD opens at forty-five
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia's LinkedIn article gives 19 May 2011, 45 dollars a share, NYSE, ticker LNKD, first-day close 94.25 and a gain of more than 109 percent. A working note giving a 171 percent close was a garbled rendering of the intraday high.
stops.campa: LinkedIn prices its shares at forty-five dollars and lists on the New York Stock Exchange on the nineteenth of May 2011, eight years and two weeks after the site opened to nobody in particular. The stock touches roughly a hundred and twenty-two dollars during the day and closes at ninety-four twenty-five, up about a hundred and nine percent, the loudest first day for an American internet listing since Google. Hoffman is the controlling shareholder; contemporary estimates of his stake run between one point eight and two point three billion dollars.
suggested_refs: LinkedIn's IPO prospectus and the 19 May 2011 first-day trading record

stops.name: Redmond: Microsoft buys the network
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia's LinkedIn article gives the 13 June 2016 announcement at 196 dollars a share and 26.2 billion dollars, and the 8 December 2016 closing. The coordinate is the Microsoft Redmond campus geotag, harmonizing three working pins that had scattered up to three and a half kilometres.
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of June 2016 Microsoft announces it will buy LinkedIn outright, all cash, one hundred and ninety-six dollars a share, twenty-six point two billion dollars. It is the largest acquisition in Microsoft's history to that date. The deal closes on the eighth of December. The company he started in a living room becomes a division of the firm that made the operating system running on the machines in that living room. Just under fourteen years separate the incorporation from the closing.
suggested_refs: Microsoft and LinkedIn merger agreement, 13 June 2016

stops.name: Redmond: a seat on Microsoft's board
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia's Reid Hoffman article gives 14 March 2017 for the Microsoft board appointment. The achievement.org profile, sometimes cited for this date, carries no entry for it at all. The dossier's claim that he announced in June 2026 that he would not stand for reelection is not attested in any source reached here.
stops.campa: The sale closes on the eighth of December 2016. Three months later, on the fourteenth of March 2017, he joins Microsoft's board of directors. He is not an executive of the acquired business; he is a director of the acquirer, which is a different and stranger position for a founder to occupy, and no source reached here records anyone objecting to it. It will matter in 2024, when Microsoft takes the staff of another company he founded and he recuses himself from his own board's vote on the arrangement.
suggested_refs: Microsoft Corporation proxy statements, 2017 onward, for board composition

stops.name: MIT Media Lab, Cambridge: introduced to a donor
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; Wikipedia's Reid Hoffman article lists a July 2013 meeting with Epstein on the MIT campus. The underlying citation could not be opened directly in this pass, so the month precision rests on the encyclopedia's own summary.
stops.campa: Joi Ito, director of the MIT Media Lab, asks him to help cultivate a donor and tells him the man has cleared MIT's vetting. In July 2013 Hoffman meets Jeffrey Epstein on the MIT campus. Epstein has been a registered sex offender for five years by then, convicted in Florida in 2008 of soliciting a minor for prostitution; the conviction is public, and no account claims Hoffman is unaware of it. What he is told is that the institution has already weighed it. He goes on with the fundraising.

stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the 2 August 2015 date is dossier-only. Wikipedia's sentence placing the dinner under a 2019 heading gives the year of reporting, not of the dinner, and the two accounts are therefore compatible rather than contradictory. The guest list, as reported four years later, includes Joi Ito, Jeffrey Epstein, Peter Thiel, Elon Musk, and Mark Zuckerberg with Priscilla Chan. stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; Wikipedia gives membership since 2015. Month and day order the segment. The coordinate is the Harold Pratt House at 58 East 68th Street, correcting a working pin that drifted a hundred and eighty metres.
